1.patient_information_and_chief_complain.text: Basic information: Male patient, 51 years old, construction worker (for 2 years), previously engaged in business. He was admitted to our department inpatient ward on Day 0, because of "fever with cough for more than 1 month." One month before admission, the patient developed fever, cough, sputum production, blood-streaked sputum, accompanied by headache, with a maximum temperature of 39.7℃. He presented to an outside hospital on Day -18. Blood tests showed elevated white blood cell count, neutrophil percentage, and C-reactive protein (>200mg/L), albumin 26g/L, and serum sodium 127mmol/L. Non-contrast chest CT indicated a lesion in the right middle lobe and scattered nodules in both lungs. Tumor markers and T-SPOT showed no obvious abnormalities. Cephalosporin antibiotics were given for anti-infective treatment without improvement. Meanwhile, at the time of admission to the local hospital, antinuclear antibody + ANCA and other autoantibody tests were sent to a third-party laboratory, and all results returned negative. Past medical history and personal history were unremarkable. First biopsy: bronchoscopy. On Day -14, bronchoscopy was completed, showing a neoplasm at the orifice of the right middle lobe bronchus, with the lumen basically completely obstructed. Six biopsy samples were taken from the right middle lobe bronchial orifice, and brushing and lavage fluid culture were also performed. No special pathogen was identified in the lavage fluid culture. Pathology result: Microscopy showed chronic active inflammation of the mucosa with extensive necrosis and hemorrhage, without definite evidence of malignancy. Second biopsy, again by bronchoscopy. On Day -10, the local hospital again completed bronchoscopy: a neoplasm was seen at the orifice of the right middle lobe bronchus, with the lumen basically completely obstructed. Seven biopsy samples were taken from the right middle lobe bronchial orifice, and brushing and lavage were again performed; pathology showed no evidence of malignant tumor or granulomatous inflammation, and acid-fast staining was negative. Lavage fluid culture showed no obvious abnormalities. On Day -8, after 10 days of active anti-infective treatment, repeat chest CT suggested: right middle lobe consolidation with multiple nodules in both lungs, lung cancer with multiple intrapulmonary metastases considered more likely; small bilateral pleural effusions. Third bronchoscopic biopsy. Bronchoscopy on Day -8, showed: a neoplasm at the orifice of the right middle lobe bronchus causing luminal obstruction. Eight biopsies were taken from the right middle lobe bronchial orifice and intraluminally, with brushing performed, and lavage at the right middle lobe bronchial orifice; the lavage fluid was sent for mNGS. Pathology still showed no evidence of malignant tumor or granulomatous inflammation; acid-fast staining (-); only ciliated columnar epithelial cells, lymphocytes, neutrophils, and a small number of mildly atypical cells were seen. Lavage fluid NGS indicated Klebsiella pneumoniae, reads 18394, with no evidence of fungi or TB. The outside hospital gave tigecycline + amikacin for anti-infective treatment for more than 10 days, without obvious improvement, and chest tightness worsened, with occasional hemoptysis. He was referred to our hospital for further diagnosis and treatment. Consultation result at our hospital for the second outside hospital pathology (right middle lung): bronchial mucosal epithelium was seen on the surface in some areas, most areas consisted of inflammatory exudate and necrotic material with marked neutrophilic infiltration, and inflammatory granulation tissue at the base, consistent with acute and chronic inflammation; our hospital consultation conclusion for the third outside hospital pathology: microscopy showed inflammatory exudate and necrotic material with many inflammatory cells, inflammatory granulation tissue at the base, and occasional multinucleated giant cells, consistent with acute and chronic inflammation. The patient presented to our hospital on Day -1, 20 days after disease onset, and was first kept for observation in the emergency department. At that time, tests showed: hemoglobin 120g/L, platelets 360X10^9/L, white blood cells 10.48X10^9/L, neutrophil percentage 94.3%, D-dimer 4.81mg/L, albumin 28g/L, alanine aminotransferase 207U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 47U/L, γ-glutamyl transferase 274U/L, sodium 129mmol/L, potassium 5.0mmol/L, C-reactive protein >90.0mg/L, N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide 276.6pg/mL, procalcitonin: 0.25ng/mL. Chest and abdominal CT: right lung MT with inflammation, possible bilateral lung metastases, slightly enlarged right hilar and mediastinal lymph nodes, small right pleural effusion; trace pelvic effusion. Pulmonary artery CTA: occlusion of the right middle lobe pulmonary artery, narrowing of partial branches of both pulmonary arteries; small possible embolus in a branch of the left lower pulmonary artery. In the emergency department, meropenem was given for anti-infective treatment, atomolan for liver protection, low-molecular-weight heparin for anticoagulation, and other treatment. He still had fever, chest tightness, cough, hemoptysis, etc., and was admitted to our respiratory ward for further treatment. Since disease onset, the patient had fair general condition, poor appetite, acceptable sleep at night, no special abnormalities in urination or defecation, and recent weight loss of 8kg. Physical examination: T: 37.1℃ P: 100/min R: 19/min BP: 102/66 mmHg SPO2 90% (without oxygen). On percussion of both lungs, the right lung was dull; on auscultation, breath sounds in the right lung were decreased, without obvious dry or wet rales or wheezing. Local conjunctival hyperemia and a small amount of blood crusting in the nasal cavity were noted. Laboratory examinations: T-SPOT negative, cryptococcal capsular antigen test negative, tumor markers: NSE 25.5, others normal. White blood cell count and CRP were elevated, D-dimer was elevated, albumin was decreased, and liver function was mildly abnormal; urinalysis was normal, urine protein negative. G test 19.3, GM test 0.157; BNP 380pg/mL. HIV and syphilis were negative, and cellular immunity was normal.

differential_diagnoses.name: Primary lung cancer (central type, with possible obstructive pneumonia/intrapulmonary metastasis)
supporting_evidence: Chest CT showed "right lung malignant tumor with inflammation, possible bilateral pulmonary metastases, slightly enlarged right hilar and mediastinal lymph nodes, and a small right pleural effusion"; repeat CT at an outside hospital showed "consolidation in the right middle lobe with multiple nodules in both lungs, highly suggestive of lung cancer with multiple intrapulmonary metastatic lesions"
All 3 bronchoscopies showed "a new growth at the orifice of the right middle lobe bronchus, with the lumen basically completely obstructed/occluded"

The patient has persistent fever, cough, sputum production, blood-streaked sputum/occasional hemoptysis, chest tightness, and a recent weight loss of 8 kg, which are consistent with common manifestations of pulmonary malignancy.
Imaging shows a large area of consolidation/mass-like lesion predominantly in the right middle lobe, with multiple nodular opacities in both lungs.
Secondary infection caused by the tumor may explain the marked elevation of the white blood cell count, neutrophil percentage, and CRP, as well as the poor response to anti-infective therapy.
opposing_evidence: Pathology from 3 bronchoscopic biopsies and brushings all showed "no definite evidence of malignancy / no evidence of malignant tumor"
Tumor markers: all were normal except for NSE 25.5; T-SPOT showed no abnormality
Multiple pathology examinations mainly showed inflammatory exudative necrotic material, acute and chronic inflammation, and inflammatory granulation tissue, rather than definite tumor tissue.

differential_diagnoses.name: Obstructive pneumonia/lung abscess
supporting_evidence: The illness onset was characterized mainly by "fever accompanied by cough for more than 1 month," with a maximum temperature of 39.7℃, accompanied by productive cough and blood-streaked sputum.
Inflammatory markers were markedly elevated: leukocyte count and neutrophil percentage were increased, and CRP remained >90mg/L after previously being >200mg/L

The pathology from all 3 biopsies was predominantly described as "chronic active inflammation with extensive necrosis and hemorrhage," "inflammatory exudate and necrotic debris," "prominent neutrophilic infiltration," and "acute and chronic inflammation."
Bronchoscopy showed obstruction of the right middle lobe bronchial orifice, which may lead to post-obstructive infection.
mNGS of the lavage fluid indicated "Klebsiella pneumoniae, 18394 reads"
Imaging shows a large area of consolidation in the right middle lobe/adjacent to the right hilum, consistent with necrotizing pneumonia or postobstructive pneumonia.
opposing_evidence: After sequential anti-infective treatment with cephalosporins, tigecycline + amikacin, meropenem, etc., there was "no obvious improvement".
Repeated lavage fluid cultures showed "no specific pathogens detected/no obvious abnormalities," suggesting that the evidence for a routine infection is insufficient.
Multiple nodules in both lungs, mildly enlarged lymph nodes in the right hilum and mediastinum, and an 8 kg weight loss cannot be fully explained by simple bacterial pneumonia

differential_diagnoses.name: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) or ANCA-negative pulmonary vasculitis
supporting_evidence: Systemic inflammatory manifestations such as fever, hemoptysis/blood-streaked sputum, headache, and weight loss are present
Localized conjunctival redness and a small amount of blood crusting in the nasal cavity, suggesting possible upper respiratory tract/ocular involvement

Chest imaging shows "multiple nodules in both lungs," and pulmonary artery CTA showed "occlusion of the right middle lobe pulmonary artery and narrowing of some branches of both pulmonary arteries," which can be seen in pulmonary vasculitic lesions.

Biopsy pathology showed necrotizing inflammation and inflammatory granulation tissue, and also mentioned "occasional multinucleated giant cells," which has some overlap with necrotizing granulomatous inflammation.
Poor response to anti-infective treatment, not supporting a simple common bacterial infection
opposing_evidence: Outside-hospital autoantibody testing, including ANA and ANCA, was "all negative"
Pathology from 3 bronchoscopies: "No granulomatous inflammatory structures identified"
Urinalysis was normal, urine protein was negative, and no clear evidence of renal involvement was seen in the first stage.

differential_diagnoses.name: Pulmonary tuberculosis or bronchial tuberculosis (with endobronchial granulomatous lesions)
supporting_evidence: Has manifestations seen in TB such as fever, cough, sputum production, hemoptysis, and weight loss
Repeated bronchoscopy showed a neoplasm at the orifice of the right middle lobe bronchus with obstruction; endobronchial TB can present as an intraluminal neoplasm-like lesion and obstruction.
Multiple nodules in both lungs and a small right pleural effusion can occur in TB
Pathology shows necrotizing inflammation and inflammatory granulation tissue; imaging also shows consolidation and nodules, which may overlap with TB
opposing_evidence: All 3 pathology examinations showed “no granulomatous inflammatory structures identified,” and acid-fast staining was negative.
mNGS of lavage fluid: "no evidence of TB detected"
No specific pathogen was detected in lavage fluid culture

differential_diagnoses.name: Invasive fungal infection or other rare opportunistic infections (such as Aspergillus, Mucor, etc.)
supporting_evidence: The patient has persistent high fever, hemoptysis, chest imaging showing consolidation with multiple nodules, and a poor response to conventional antibacterial therapy.
On bronchoscopy, neoplasm-like intraluminal obstruction is seen; fungal infection can form necrotic pseudomembranes or granulomatous lesions.
Pathology repeatedly showed necrosis and acute and chronic inflammation, consistent with the histologic background of some invasive fungal infections
Imaging shows a large lesion in the right lung and scattered nodules in both lungs, which can be seen in invasive fungal infection.
opposing_evidence: HIV-negative, with normal cellular immunity; the first stage did not indicate a definite immunosuppressive background.
G test 19.3, GM test 0.157, cryptococcal capsular antigen negative
Lavage fluid mNGS: "No evidence of fungi detected"

differential_diagnoses.name: Pulmonary thromboembolism/tumor embolism with pulmonary infarction
supporting_evidence: Pulmonary artery CTA showed: "occlusion of the right middle lobe pulmonary artery, narrowing of some branches of both pulmonary arteries; possible small emboli in branches of the left lower pulmonary artery"
Elevated D-dimer 4.81 mg/L
The patient has chest tightness, hemoptysis, and hypoxemia (SpO2 90% on room air).
Imaging images show changes in the right lung lesion adjacent to the vascular region, a small right pleural effusion, and pleural effusion and hemoptysis may occur in pulmonary infarction
opposing_evidence: Persistent high fever for more than 1 month, markedly elevated CRP, significant endobronchial neoplastic obstruction, and multiple nodules in both lungs suggest that thromboembolism alone cannot fully explain all manifestations.
Bronchoscopy and pathology mainly suggest localized necrotizing inflammation and an intraluminal obstructive lesion, rather than a purely embolic disease.

stage2_input.text: On Day +4, an ultrasound-guided percutaneous lung biopsy was performed. Intraoperatively, a hypoechoic mass measuring approximately 142×81 mm was seen in the right lung. Three tissue biopsy cores (10-20 mm in length) were obtained and sent for pathology and lung tissue culture. Lung tissue culture: smear showed no fungi, bacteria, or acid-fast bacilli. Pathology: microscopy showed completely necrotic tissue with abundant degenerative acute and chronic inflammatory cell infiltration; special stains showed residual alveoli; no definite tumor tissue was identified, favoring an infarct lesion. Immunohistochemistry: CK{pan} (epithelial+), CD68{KP1} (histiocytes+), CD3 (partial lymphocytes+), CD20(-), CD56(-). Special stains: PAS(-), acid-fast(-), GMS(-), reticulin stain (showing residual alveolar framework). Others: (in situ hybridization) EBER(-). The fifth bronchoscopy pathological biopsy was still obtained by bronchoscopy. Bronchoscopy showed edematous and rough mucosa of the right main bronchus and right bronchus intermedius, with diffuse surface necrosis; the right middle lobe bronchial orifice was obstructed by necrotic tissue, and the lumen was nearly occluded. Using radial ultrasound, a hypoechoic area was detected through the distal right middle lobe; combined with fluoroscopy, TBLB and brushings were performed at multiple points in this lesion. On-site rapid pathological evaluation, ROSE smear (right middle lobe), showed abundant necrosis and inflammatory cells. In view of the findings in the right main bronchus and right bronchus intermedius, biopsy and brushing of the necrotic mucosa in the right bronchus intermedius were performed under direct visualization; ROSE smear (right bronchus intermedius) showed abundant neutrophils, histiocytes, and some multinucleated giant cells. Lavage was performed in the right middle and lower lobes and sent for bacterial, fungal, and TB smears and cultures, GM, and mNGS. Lung tissue culture: smear still showed no fungi, bacteria, or acid-fast bacilli; XPERT Mycobacterium tuberculosis DNA: negative. Lavage fluid culture: smear showed no fungi, bacteria, or acid-fast bacilli; culture showed no Haemophilus parahaemolyticus group, with scant growth of viridans streptococci; XPERT negative; GM assay and qualitative cryptococcal capsular antigen test both showed no positive results. Lung tissue mNGS results: biopsy tissue showed Streptococcus pneumoniae (Reads=6), Malassezia restricta (Reads=32), and Rothia dentocariosa (Reads=122); lavage fluid showed Staphylococcus haemolyticus (Reads=6), Malassezia restricta (Reads=22), Serratia grimesii (Reads=69), Haemophilus parainfluenzae (Reads=78), Staphylococcus hominis (Reads=123), Rothia dentocariosa (Reads=187), Moraxella osloensis (Reads=212), and Rhodococcus erythropolis (Reads=212). Cytopathology smears: (right middle lobe) smear showed abundant coagulative necrosis; tuberculous necrosis could not be excluded; (right bronchus intermedius) smear showed some inflammatory cells, a small number of suspicious epithelioid cells, and multinucleated giant cells; granulomatous lesion could not be excluded. Pathology results: (right middle lobe of lung) all biopsy tissue was necrotic on microscopy; special stains showed no positive organisms; no definite tumor tissue was identified, favoring an infarct lesion. Right bronchus intermedius biopsy: most of the biopsy tissue was necrotic on microscopy, with a small amount of inflammatory granulation tissue also seen; combined with the immunohistochemistry results, no tumor tissue was identified.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: We subsequently completed ANCA testing at our hospital, which showed: cANCA (+), pANCA (-), PR3 >200 RU/mL; MPO <2.00.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient presented with persistent fever, cough with sputum production, blood-streaked sputum/hemoptysis, weight loss, chest CT showing multiple nodules in both lungs and a large lesion in the right lung, and pulmonary artery CTA showing occlusion/narrowing of branches of the right middle lobe pulmonary artery. Pathology repeatedly indicated extensive necrosis, inflammatory granulation tissue, and multinucleated giant cells, but tumor was never confirmed and no specific pathogen was identified. At the same time, there were clues of conjunctival injection, nasal blood crusting, headache, delirium, and sinusitis, suggesting multisystem involvement of the lungs-upper airway-eyes-nervous system, with vasculitis, especially GPA, being highly suspected. Although third-party autoantibodies at an outside hospital were previously negative, given the high clinical suspicion and disease progression, repeat testing at our hospital and quantitative PR3/MPO testing are needed. This testing is intended to resolve the key diagnostic question of whether ANCA-associated vasculitis is present, and is निर्णative for establishing GPA, excluding a disease course primarily driven by simple infection or malignancy, and determining whether immunosuppressive therapy such as high-dose glucocorticoids and cyclophosphamide can be initiated in a timely manner.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: PET/CT performed on Day +12: inflammatory lesions possibly involving the left lacrimal gland, nasal cavity, multiple paranasal sinuses, nasopharynx, bilateral parotid glands, both lungs, prostate, and multiple lymph nodes (parapharyngeal space, bilateral neck, supraclavicular region, mediastinum, and bilateral hila); lymphoma involvement remains to be excluded. Possible reactive splenic enlargement; lymphoma involvement remains to be excluded.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient's pulmonary lesions are complex: a neoplasm-like endobronchial obstruction in the right middle lobe, multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules, hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy, and marked weight loss; multiple anti-infective treatments were ineffective, and prior imaging at one point was highly suspicious for lung cancer with intrapulmonary metastases. On the other hand, multiple pathology examinations showed only necrotizing inflammation and inflammatory granulation tissue, suggesting a possible systemic inflammatory disease. PET/CT is used to assess the distribution and metabolic activity of the lesions at the whole-body level and to determine whether there are extrapulmonary sites of involvement, especially the lacrimal glands, nasal cavity/paranasal sinuses, nasopharynx, parotid glands, lymph nodes, and spleen; if these sites are involved simultaneously, this would more strongly support systemic inflammation/vasculitis rather than a solitary pulmonary infection. The clinical questions this examination is intended to address include: differentiating inflammatory lesions from neoplastic diseases such as lymphoma/metastatic tumors, identifying a more suitable site for biopsy sampling, determining whether the lesions represent multisystem involvement, and thereby increasing diagnostic confidence, reducing blind repetitive invasive pulmonary sampling, and guiding subsequent assessment of the extent of treatment.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: The final pathology result from the Department of Pathology (fifth bronchoscopy) was: biopsy tissue from the right intermediate bronchus showed that most of the tissue was necrotic on microscopic examination, with a small amount of inflammatory granulation tissue also seen. Immunohistochemistry findings suggested proliferation of both T and B lymphocytes within the biopsy tissue, accompanied by extensive neutrophil infiltration and large areas of tissue necrosis, favoring an inflammatory lesion.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient had persistent high fever, cough with sputum production, hemoptysis, chest tightness, and hypoxemia. Imaging showed a large lesion in the right middle lobe with multiple nodules in both lungs, and bronchoscopy repeatedly revealed a neoplasm-like lesion at the orifice of the right middle lobe bronchus with necrotic material causing obstruction, with the lumen nearly occluded. These findings suggest marked local disease activity and also pose risks of airway obstruction and post-obstructive infection. Multiple previous evaluations failed to establish a definite diagnosis, while the disease course progressed rapidly and the response to anti-infective treatment was poor. Repeat bronchoscopy was therefore required to directly visualize the morphology of the lesion, assess the extent of necrosis and obstruction, and repeatedly obtain specimens from more representative sites under direct visualization, while also completing brush cytology, lavage, and submission for pathogen testing. The issues this examination needed to resolve were: whether the lesion was a tumor, infection, or necrotizing inflammation/vasculitis; whether there was airway necrosis that could explain the hemoptysis and hypoxemia; and whether histologic evidence sufficient to support treatment decision-making could be obtained. The bronchoscopy results were directly related to the diagnostic pathway and would provide a key basis for whether to subsequently initiate steroid pulse therapy and immunosuppressive treatment.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: The final pathology result from the Department of Pathology (fifth bronchoscopy) was: biopsy tissue from the right intermediate bronchus showed that most of the tissue was necrotic on microscopic examination, with a small amount of inflammatory granulation tissue also seen. Immunohistochemistry findings suggested proliferation of both T and B lymphocytes within the biopsy tissue, accompanied by extensive neutrophil infiltration and large areas of tissue necrosis, favoring an inflammatory lesion.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient's pulmonary lesions showed a mass/neoplasm-like appearance on both imaging and microscopy. At the outside hospital and in the early stage at our hospital, the key priorities were to exclude central lung cancer, lymphoma, TB, fungal infection, and other special infections, but repeated microbiologic and pathologic evaluations remained inconclusive. In this context, biopsy of the most abnormal area of the right intermediate bronchus, where necrosis was most pronounced, with histopathologic examination, was performed to obtain direct histologic evidence and determine whether malignant tumor cells, granulomatous inflammation, vasculitis-related necrotizing inflammation, or infarct-like changes were present. This examination primarily addressed the question of the 'nature of the lesion': whether the lack of response to repeated anti-infective therapy meant it was truly not an infection; why imaging was highly suspicious for tumor despite repeatedly negative results; and whether pulmonary artery occlusion and multiple nodules were related to necrotizing inflammatory disease. Pathology suggested extensive necrosis and inflammatory granulation tissue without tumor; together with the systemic clinical clues, this helped support GPA rather than tumor or TB and guided subsequent immunotherapy.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: The final pathology result from the Department of Pathology (fifth bronchoscopy) was: biopsy tissue from the right intermediate bronchus showed that most of the tissue was necrotic on microscopic examination, with a small amount of inflammatory granulation tissue also seen. Immunohistochemistry findings suggested proliferation of both T and B lymphocytes within the biopsy tissue, accompanied by extensive neutrophil infiltration and large areas of tissue necrosis, favoring an inflammatory lesion.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: Because the biopsy specimen in this case contained a very large amount of necrotic material, HE morphology alone was inherently limited. Meanwhile, the patient's pulmonary and systemic manifestations simultaneously strongly suggested multiple possibilities, including malignant tumor, lymphoproliferative disease, and necrotizing inflammatory disease. Therefore, immunohistochemistry was additionally required to further analyze the cellular components and the nature of the lesion. Its main clinical purposes included: determining whether there were abnormal cell populations related to epithelial tumor or lymphoma; distinguishing reactive T- and B-lymphocytic hyperplasia from neoplastic infiltration; and, in the context of abundant neutrophilic infiltration and necrosis, evaluating whether the lesion was more consistent with inflammation or tumor. This examination is helpful at the pathologic level for excluding important differential diagnoses, strengthening the chain of evidence for an 'inflammatory lesion/vasculitis-related necrotizing lesion,' thereby reducing the risk of inappropriate antitumor therapy, and providing pathologic support for subsequent regimens such as high-dose glucocorticoids and cyclophosphamide.

7.key_confirmatory_exam_information.text: The patient's condition continued to progress, with persistent delirium, persistently elevated inflammatory markers, recurrent fever, and hyponatremia and hypoproteinemia that were difficult to correct. On Day +9, the patient developed impaired consciousness and persistent delirium; on Day +9, head CT showed no obvious evidence of intracranial metastasis; a subacute lacunar infarct in the left frontal lobe, multiple lacunar ischemic foci in the brain; and chronic sinus inflammation. On physical examination at admission, there was localized conjunctival hyperemia and a small amount of blood crusting in the nasal cavity, which gradually worsened during the subsequent hospitalization. We then completed ANCA testing at our hospital, which showed: cANCA (+), pANCA (-), PR3 >200 RU/mL; MPO <2.00. PET/CT performed on Day +12 suggested possible inflammatory involvement of the left lacrimal gland, nasal cavity, multiple paranasal sinuses, nasopharynx, bilateral parotid glands, ორივी lungs, prostate, and multiple lymph nodes (parapharyngeal space, bilateral neck, clavicular regions, mediastinum, and bilateral hila); lymphoma involvement remained to be excluded. Reactive splenic enlargement was also possible, and lymphoma involvement remained to be excluded. At the same time, pathology also reported that FISH and genetic testing showed no evidence of lymphoma or sarcoma. The final pathology result from the Department of Pathology was as follows (fifth bronchoscopy): (right intermediate bronchus) most of the biopsy tissue was necrotic on microscopy, with a small amount of inflammatory granulation tissue also seen. Immunohistochemistry suggested proliferation of both T and B lymphocytes in the biopsy tissue, with abundant neutrophilic infiltration and extensive tissue necrosis, favoring an inflammatory lesion. Possible Wegener granulomatosis was considered.

8.final_diagnosis_and_diagnostic_basis.final_diagnosis: ANCA-associated vasculitis: granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener granulomatosis) involving multiple organ systems (nervous system, lacrimal glands, nasal cavity, both lungs, etc.)
diagnostic_basis: Clinical manifestations: fever, cough, hemoptysis, chest tightness, localized conjunctival redness, a small amount of blood crusting in the nasal cavity, persistent delirium; poor response to anti-infective therapy
Laboratory tests: cANCA (+), pANCA (-), PR3 >200 RU/mL

Imaging studies: chest CT: right middle lobe consolidation with multiple nodules in both lungs; PET/CT suggested inflammatory lesions involving the left lacrimal gland, nasal cavity, multiple paranasal sinus groups, nasopharynx, bilateral parotid glands, both lungs, prostate, and multiple lymph nodes; head CT suggested chronic inflammation of the sinuses

Pathologic examination: Most of the biopsy tissue is necrotic on microscopy; in addition, a small amount of inflammatory granulation tissue is present. Immunohistochemistry results suggest proliferation of both T and B lymphocytes within the biopsy tissue, accompanied by extensive neutrophil infiltration and large areas of tissue necrosis, favoring an inflammatory lesion.

treatment_plan: Methylprednisolone 1 g QD pulse therapy for 3 days, followed by 80 mg Q8H for 3 days, followed by 40 mg Q8H for 3 days, followed by 40 mg Q12H, then changed to oral 30 mg BID
Adjunctive albumin and gamma globulin 20 g × 5 days
On Day +24, cyclophosphamide 0.4 g was administered by intravenous infusion.
treatment_response: On the day of corticosteroid pulse therapy, the patient's mental status improved, delirium symptoms improved, and body temperature decreased.
After 3 days, inflammatory markers decreased, hypoproteinemia and hyponatremia improved, epistaxis stopped, and oxygenation improved
The patient's condition stabilized and improved, and the patient was discharged.
